author: jeffling
message: feat(postgres_cdc): Postgres CDC source plugin via supabase/etl (#7) * feat(postgres_cdc): Postgres CDC source plugin via supabase/etl Streams Postgres logical-replication changes (initial table copy + continuous CDC) by embedding the supabase/etl pipeline. Output schema is the replicated table's own columns plus _gs_op; delivery is at-least-once with deferred-ack checkpointing. Sources sharing a slot_name share one replication slot (coordinated fan-out). Extracted from streamling-goldsky-plugins research/supabase-etl-source (commits e78a04d..446dfa0, 30 commits). Adapted to the community crate: register_plugin_source! wiring, sqlx 'postgres' feature, etl/secrecy/chrono/base64/sha2 deps, rustc 1.93.1 (supabase/etl MSRV), and goldsky_plugins -> community_plugins in tests/docs. E2e tests self-skip without E2E_POSTGRES_CDC_URL. Verified locally: cargo check --all-targets, cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy -D warnings, 88 lib unit tests pass. * feat(postgres_cdc): address review, add auto_create_publication Review feedback (@sap1ens): - drop stale design-doc reference in mod.rs - rename shared.rs -> pipeline.rs (it's a pipeline registry) - rename bridge `Unit` -> `WriteUnit` - document that PostgresStore + an `etl` schema live in the source DB - README: Postgres >= 14 minimum, schema evolution unsupported, REPLICA IDENTITY FULL recommendation Auto-publication: - new `auto_create_publication` option (default false): before pipeline start, create the publication if missing or ALTER ... ADD TABLE any registered tables not yet in it; no-op for FOR ALL TABLES. Needs CREATE on the database / table ownership. Extracted a shared pg_connect_options helper from discovery. Tests: - unit: auto_create_publication parsing; identifier quoting - e2e: auto_create_publication_creates_and_streams (no pre-created pub) * ci: run postgres_cdc e2e in CI; fix parallel-test slot collision - Wire a postgres:16 container with wal_level=logical into the plugin-e2e job and set E2E_POSTGRES_CDC_URL so the postgres_cdc_source e2e tests actually run instead of self-skipping (the reviewer asked to confirm these run). - Give the auto-create e2e test a distinct slot_name prefix. Both source tests derived slot_name from a millisecond nonce; under parallel execution they could hit the same pipeline id and collide on the process-global pipeline registry (mismatched publication -> new() rejected). Distinct prefixes make the registry keys and PG slots unique regardless of nonce. * ci: reuse the existing logical-replication Postgres for CDC e2e The shared e2e Postgres (streamling infra/local-k8s/postgres.yaml) already runs postgres:16 with wal_level=logical and is exposed via E2E_POSTGRES_URL by k3s-setup.sh --env-only. Alias E2E_POSTGRES_CDC_URL to it instead of spinning up a second container. * test: scope shared-slot assertion to the group's own apply slot The shared-slot e2e asserted exactly one supabase_etl_apply_% slot, but that counts every group's apply slot in the shared e2e Postgres. Under nextest's parallel, cross-binary execution the other postgres_cdc tests create their own apply slots in the same DB, so the count exceeded one and the assertion failed in CI. Count only this group's slot (supabase_etl_apply_<hash_slot_name(slot)>) instead. Expose hash_slot_name from the postgres_cdc module so the integration test can derive the expected slot name. * feat(postgres_cdc): default auto_create_publication to true; document role permissions - Flip the auto_create_publication default from false to true so the publication is created/managed out of the box. Operators who manage the publication themselves set auto_create_publication: false. - README: add a Permissions section with example SQL for a least-privilege REPLICATION role (CONNECT, USAGE, SELECT for the copy; CREATE on the database; table ownership to add tables to a publication), and note the opt-out for manually-managed publications. * ci(serde): serialize postgres_cdc e2e tests in nextest The postgres_cdc e2e tests share one Postgres database. etl's source migrations (CREATE SCHEMA etl, ...) are not concurrency-safe, so when nextest started the three pipelines in parallel one aborted with 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint pg_namespace_nspname_index' during store init (flaky in CI). Assign the postgres_cdc test binaries to a max-threads=1 nextest test group so they run one at a time. * ci: trigger on .config/** changes (nextest config) * feat: make memory backpressure configurable * fix: linting --------- Co-authored-by: streamling-bot <dev@goldsky.io> Co-authored-by: Yaroslav Tkachenko <sapiensy@gmail.com>

author: jeffling
message: feat(clickhouse): adaptive sort-key-range source pagination (#16) * feat(clickhouse): adaptive sort-key-range source pagination The source query wrapped its scan in an ORDER BY on the sorting key, which forced read-in-order on the main table and made ClickHouse skip any matching projection (read-in-order is not supported on projections). Drop the ORDER BY and paginate deterministically by disjoint half-open ranges on the first sorting key, so a projection can be selected. - RangeController owns the range cursor and adapts range width from each page's row count and elapsed time. A LIMIT page_size+1 tripwire detects an overflowing range and re-reads it smaller with no duplicates (the response is buffered before emit); a soft time budget shrinks before the hard query timeout. - An up-front count() probe sizes the first range from observed density. - The checkpoint cursor is the range start, so restart re-reads at most the in-flight range (at-least-once, covered by sink dedup). - Rename config block_range -> sort_key_range (env STREAMLING__CLICKHOUSE_SOURCE__SORT_KEY_RANGE). Breaking change. Data-loss coverage: unit tests assert the emitted ranges tile the key space with no gaps and every row exactly once under overflow, timeout, and width down/up rescaling; e2e tests verify completeness against ClickHouse. * feat(clickhouse): version-aware source dedup for ReplacingMergeTree The ClickHouse source emits raw rows in scan order (no ORDER BY, so a matching projection is usable). For ReplacingMergeTree tables this means duplicate versions of each ORDER BY key reach downstream in arbitrary order, so the existing position-based dedup picks the wrong winner. Infer the version column from system.tables.engine_full (parse_replacing_merge_tree_dedup handles Shared/Replicated/plain Replacing variants by dropping the quoted path/replica args), and deduplicate each fully-read page by max version before emission. Keys whose max-version row is a tombstone (_gs_op='d') are dropped (FINAL semantics). All versions of a key share the first sorting key so they land in one page, making per-page coalescing complete and correct. - dedup util: deduplicate_record_batch(s)_by_version + TombstoneRule (max-version wins; ties break by position; hash collisions resolved by real PK equality, STRM-5990 style; tombstone match is type-safe via a literal array + make_comparator, no per-row ScalarValue alloc) - 6 version-aware dedup unit tests + 6 engine-parser unit tests * fix(clickhouse): force-include version col so dedup activates with explicit columns Dedup was silently disabled whenever the configured columns omitted the inferred version column — most notably the hybrid source path, where ClickHouseSchemaAdapter::get_columns projects ClickHouse to the Kafka target schema (which excludes ClickHouse housekeeping columns like insert_timestamp and is_deleted). The line-384 schema gate flunked the inference and the source emitted raw, undeduped rows. Decouple the internal scan schema from the external provider schema: - new_source now infers the version column from engine_full first, then appends it to the scan column list when the configured columns omit it ("*" already includes everything, so no append). On a fetch_schema failure we fall back to the configured columns with dedup disabled — one extra startup query in the rare invalid-version case, none in the common case. - SourceParams carries project_out_version_index: Option<usize> — set only when we force-included the version column. - The execute() emission projects that column out of every emitted batch via project_out_column, so the stream's external schema (and the hybrid union's schema contract) is unchanged. - The inference log is moved alongside the provider-schema computation and now reports whether force-inclusion was needed; the disabled-case log distinguishes 'not selectable' from 'no Replacing engine'. Test SourceParams construction updated for the new field. Existing dedup/parser tests still pass (30 + 241). * test(clickhouse): e2e regression for ReplacingMergeTree dedup with explicit columns Adds test_clickhouse_source_replacing_dedup_when_version_column_not_selected, which replays the hybrid-source projection (configured columns omit insert_timestamp / is_deleted) that previously silently disabled source dedup. Five scenarios in 9 raw rows probe distinct dedup properties: - single version (sanity); - newer insert_timestamp inserted second (max-version wins); - newer insert_timestamp inserted FIRST (position-based dedup picks the wrong row; version-aware picks the right one deterministically); - tombstone is the max-version row (whole key dropped, FINAL); - tombstone older than the live row (key kept as alive). Five assertions: row count = 4 (FINAL); 'c_new' wins for id='c'; id='d' is absent; id='e' kept as 'e_alive'; and the external schema does not include insert_timestamp / is_deleted (force-included column projected out before emission). Local execution required (k3s + postgres + clickhouse): cargo check + just lint pass here; the k3s cluster in this worktree is unhealthy so the test must be run locally with 'just e2e-test test_clickhouse_source_replacing_dedup_when_version_column_not_selected' before merge. * fix(clickhouse): guard page byte size to prevent Arrow 2GiB array panic The ClickHouse source bounded pages by row count only (page_size, default 10M). On a complete page from a ReplacingMergeTree, version dedup coalesces the whole page via concat_batches into one RecordBatch; a dense Utf8/Binary column then exceeds Arrow's i32 per-array offset limit (~2GiB) and GenericBytesBuilder panics with "byte array offset overflow". Observed on matic_raw_logs in production: a page fine by rows blew the limit on bytes. Add a byte tripwire alongside the row tripwire: - MAX_PAGE_BYTES = i32::MAX / 2 (~1GiB). The widest column <= page total, so keeping the page well under i32::MAX guarantees no column overflows during concat_batches (dedup) or the IPC read. - A page over rows OR bytes shrinks width and re-reads the SAME range (cursor not advanced -> exactly-once preserved); at min width it surfaces an error instead of dropping data. Make RangeController byte-aware to avoid thrash: on_byte_overflow sizes the next width from observed byte density (one-step convergence), and on_complete clamps growth by byte density so a byte-dense region can't snap width back past the limit every cycle (row multiplier is blind to bytes and would oscillate overflow<->re-read forever). Regression tests: precise byte sizing, anti-thrash clamp, and a no-data-loss full scan through a byte-dense burst. * fix(clickhouse): target 90% of byte limit to converge in one step on_byte_overflow sized the re-read to land at exactly max_page_bytes, but a shrunk sub-range has different byte density than the page that overflowed, so it repeatedly landed a hair over the limit and shrank by one width unit per read. On matic_raw_logs this crept: width 2533 -> 2218 -> 2122 -> 2113 -> 2108 -> 2106 -> 2105 over 6 discarded ~1GiB reads before completing. Target BYTE_TARGET_RATIO (0.9) of the limit in both on_byte_overflow and on_complete's byte clamp. The 10% headroom absorbs density variance so the re-read lands under the limit in one step; even when variance exceeds it, convergence is geometric (each step shrinks >10%), not a unit creep. Updated the precise-sizing and anti-thrash tests for the new target. * fix(hybrid): skip offset-provider work in job mode to unblock termination In job mode, advance_to_next_phase ran the offset-provider transition work (a ClickHouse max-offset query + Kafka offset seeding + state save) for the unbounded phase before the hybrid execute loop's job_mode break. That phase never runs in job mode, so the work is wasted; worse, under load any of those steps stalling blocks advance_to_next_phase, which the loop must return from before it can break and end the source stream — so the sinks never complete and the job hangs. This was latent: it only surfaced once the byte-overflow guard let the bounded ClickHouse scan actually finish (previously it panicked). Guard the offset-provider block with !job_mode so the transition query and seed are skipped in job mode; phase bookkeeping and save_state still run (state stays consistent). The bounded source's own cursor is already persisted via its checkpoint Finalizer, so skipping the unbounded offset seed is safe. Regression test: advance past the bounded phase with a FailingOffsetProvider in job_mode must succeed (offset provider never called); without the skip it would propagate the injected error. * chore(clickhouse): reduce default page_size 10M -> 2M Smaller pages bound per-page memory and reduce the byte-overflow thrash window (fewer rows per page means a dense string column is less likely to approach the 2GiB Arrow array limit before the byte tripwire catches it). 2M keeps throughput reasonable while cutting peak page memory ~5x. * fix(clickhouse): flush buffered checkpoint markers before source shutdown The source's checkpointing task buffers Markers/Finalizers into a shared checkpoint_buffer and attach_checkpoints drains them onto outgoing data batches. But after the scan loop exits, the buffer was never flushed — a Marker that arrived during the final pages (or after the last data batch) had no batch to ride and was dropped when tx dropped. The sink never saw that epoch, never acked, and the coordinator stalled on "missing sinks" indefinitely — the production job-mode termination hang. After the checkpointing task shuts down (so no more messages arrive), drain checkpoint_buffer and emit a synthetic empty batch carrying any buffered markers so they reach the sink (and the hybrid safety-net) before the stream ends. The guard is dropped before the await so the spawn future stays Send. * perf(clickhouse): probe count on overflow for one-step width sizing The byte-overflow sizer divided the LIMIT-capped sample (page_size+1 rows read from the start of the range) by the full range width, under-estimating density. A dense range then shrank geometrically over many discarded multi-GiB re-reads before converging (observed ~10 steps on a dense cluster). Add RangeController::on_overflow_probed(count, observed_bytes): size the next width from the TRUE density (count/width) to satisfy both row and byte limits in one step. bytes_per_row comes from the sampled rows; multiplied by the true row density it predicts the byte density of the whole range. The method generalizes on_overflow(Some(count)) and on_byte_overflow (reduces to each when only one constraint is active). The driver probes count(*) for the overflowing range on each overflow (fetch_count gains an upper_bound param); a failed probe falls back to halving. Sparse scans are untouched (no probe except on overflow; empty pages still grow 4x). * Revert "fix(clickhouse): flush buffered checkpoint markers before source shutdown" This reverts commit d26254c375e323b486c39a0fd4c0b63bdbfa359e. * test(e2e): replicate job-mode marker-loss and multi-page termination regressions Two e2e tests that reproduce the job-mode termination hang / checkpoint marker-loss regression: 1. test_job_mode_checkpoint_epoch_finalizes: 200-row bounded ClickHouse scan with a 1s checkpoint interval forces a Marker mid-scan in job mode. Asserts process exits 0, NO 'missing sinks' / 'still waiting for finalization' warnings (markers flowed + epochs finalized), and all records in the sink. The existing 3-row test finishes before the checkpoint interval fires, so it never exercises a Marker arriving mid-scan. 2. test_job_mode_multi_page_scan_terminates: 3000-row scan with sort_key_range 500 forces multiple pages. Catches a hang or marker loss on the pagination -> completion -> flush path. * chore: address code-review feedback - fix(clickhouse): use .expect() over .unwrap() on the checkpoint-buffer mutex in the attach_checkpoints closure (RUST-001). Note: of the three sites flagged, only this one is new to the branch -- the initial range_start split.lock() pre-exists on main, and the final-flush block was already removed by the prior revert. - fix(config): add #[serde(alias = "block_range")] to sort_key_range so deployments using the old field name keep working instead of silently falling back to the 1,000,000 default. - refactor(range_controller): make on_overflow/on_byte_overflow private; the driver now calls on_overflow_probed exclusively and no caller outside the module references them. - style(dedup): add the missing blank line before hash_array_value's doc comment. * fix(clickhouse): flush buffered checkpoint markers before source shutdown The source's checkpointing task buffers Markers/Finalizers into a shared checkpoint_buffer and attach_checkpoints drains them onto outgoing data batches. But after the scan loop exits, the buffer was never flushed — a Marker that arrived during the final pages (or after the last data batch) had no batch to ride and was dropped when tx dropped. The sink never saw that epoch, never acked, and the coordinator stalled on "missing sinks" indefinitely — the production job-mode termination hang. This is a regression from the adaptive range pagination: main's keyset pagination always ended on an exhausted page that emitted an empty batch (draining the buffer); the new range pagination's last page has data and skips that drain. Fix: extract build_checkpoint_flush_batch (testable seam that drains the buffer into a synthetic empty batch carrying the markers as schema metadata) and call it after the checkpointing task shuts down, before unsubscribing. The guard is dropped before the await so the spawn future stays Send. Unit test: inject a Marker into a buffer, call build_checkpoint_flush_batch, assert the returned batch is empty (synthetic), carries the Marker in schema metadata (recoverable via extract_checkpoint_messages), and the buffer is drained. Asserts None on an empty buffer. * fix(clickhouse): derive _gs_op from the parsed is_deleted column The source hardcoded `CASE WHEN is_deleted=0 THEN 'i' ELSE 'd' END AS _gs_op`, ignoring the column name parsed from engine_full. A ReplacingMergeTree that names its deletion flag anything other than `is_deleted` (or has none) failed the read, and fetch_schema failed the same way -- it only worked because Goldsky-managed tables are always created as ReplacingMergeTree(ver, is_deleted). Thread the parsed is_deleted_column through the query builder: Some(name) derives _gs_op from that flag (so custom-named columns work); None means no engine-level deletion concept, so _gs_op is a constant 'i'. _gs_op stays always-present so the output schema contract and the _gs_op='d' tombstone rule are unchanged. fetch_schema takes the same column so its _gs_op type matches the scan's exactly. * style(clickhouse): rustfmt after is_deleted threading * fix(clickhouse): parse engine args on the matching paren, not the last parse_replacing_merge_tree_dedup used engine_full.rfind(')') to bound the engine arguments, but a real system.tables.engine_full value is 'ReplacingMergeTree(...) ORDER BY (...)' -- the trailing ORDER BY/SETTINGS clause carries its own parens, so rfind grabbed the wrong close and the ORDER BY text leaked into the parsed column names (is_deleted_column became 'is_deleted) ORDER BY (block_number'). This was masked while is_deleted_column was discarded; threading it into the _gs_op CASE expression exposed it as a SQL syntax error. Add matching_close_paren: scan with paren depth + single-quote (with '' escape) awareness to find the ')' that closes the engine's '('. Verified by a new parse test with a trailing ORDER BY clause and by the previously-failing e2e test_clickhouse_source_replacing_dedup_when_version_column_not_selected. * fix(clickhouse): use expect on mutex lock and restore 10M page_size RUST-001: split.lock().unwrap() panics on mutex poison; use .expect() with a reason so the failure is diagnosable. Restore DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE to 10M (reverts d5fbd18e's 10M->2M reduction). * fix(clickhouse): probe per-range count before the data read The adaptive range controller sized the first range from the whole-span average density, so a clustered high-fanout region (many rows per sort key) inside an otherwise-sparse span was read at the span-average width and materialised page_size+1 rows before the reactive overflow could shrink it -- the OOM path. Add a count-first sizing loop: before each data read, probe the exact row count for the current range and shrink the width to fit (new RangeController::shrink_to_fit_count). The cursor never moves during sizing, so only the upper bound shrinks; the loop re-probes until the range fits or hits min width. A probe failure is non-fatal and falls through to the existing reactive overflow. The reactive byte tripwire remains the backstop for variable-width columns. * feat(clickhouse): emit record_batch_size-bounded batches The ClickHouse source emitted whatever a deduped page held -- dedup coalesces a whole page into one RecordBatch, which can dwarf the global record_batch_size (default 1000) that the Kafka source and DataFusion operators expect. With coalesce_batches disabled, that oversized batch flowed unsplit through every transform. Thread record_batch_size into new_source (mirroring the Kafka source) and split each emitted batch into record_batch_size-row chunks at the emit point via chunk_record_batch. RecordBatch::slice shares schema and all schema metadata across chunks; checkpoint messages still ride exactly one batch -- attach_checkpoints drains its buffer on first use and no-ops on the remaining chunks of the page. Unit tests cover chunk sizes/boundaries, row order with no loss or duplication, schema-metadata preservation on every chunk, the empty and max_rows=0 edge cases, and the checkpoint-rides-first-chunk invariant. * fix(clickhouse): prefer tombstone on version tie in source dedup When a live row and a delete share the same ReplacingMergeTree version (the same insert_timestamp), the source-side version dedup picked the later-position row. The scan has no ORDER BY, so the winner was nondeterministic: a live row scanned after the delete survived and the deletion was silently lost, leaving a stale live row in the sink. On a version tie, prefer the tombstone — a delete at the same version supersedes the live row, so the key is dropped (ReplacingMergeTree FINAL with an is_deleted flag). Distinct-version and no-tombstone-rule cases are unchanged.

message: chore(skills): drop docs/CLI-grounded reference from skills The skills/ tree feeds a Bedrock KB that also ingests the published docs as a separate data source, so static reference that duplicates docs.goldsky.com or `goldsky` CLI output is redundant there and goes stale. Remove it and point to the docs / live `--help` instead. README.md and SKILLS.md listings updated. Kept deliberately: - subgraph-builder/references/schema-and-mappings.md — curated Goldsky-specific guidance (idioms/gotchas), not doc duplication - turbo-operations/data/error-patterns.json — consumed at runtime by analyze-logs.sh - datasets/data/chain-prefixes.json — stable lookup the slow/interactive CLI can't easily produce Note: sync-kb.yml syncs with --delete, so merging removes this content from the live chatbot KB. message: Address review findings: correctness, security, agent-runbook fixes Round 1 — P1 factual corrections: - VRF/nav-oracle: setFulfiller/setPublisher recovery advice was wrong (only the current role-holder can rotate, not the deployer EOA) - prediction-market: smoke test now references the configured ORACLE_WALLET_NAME instead of hardcoding the default - bitcoin-oracle: deploy-fresh branch now creates contracts/ directory before writing the .sol (the dir doesn't ship with the example) Round 2 — P2 security and gas-sponsorship correctness: - VRF/bitcoin-oracle/nav-oracle: clarify managed wallets default to sponsorGas:true on supported chains; drop unconditional faucet steps (aligns with compose/docs/solutions/.../gas-sponsorship-on-by-default) - bitcoin-oracle: warn about every-minute mainnet cron cost - solana-transactions: promote authentication:"none" warning to Non-negotiables; author: AStox
message: fix: decode getLastUpdateDetails return values in correct order (FOU-720) (#5) RedStone's MultiFeedAdapter returns (lastDataTimestamp, lastBlockTimestamp, lastValue), but we were reading index 0 as the price and index 1 as the timestamp. With lastDataTimestamp (~1.78e12) being treated as the stored price, every comparison showed ~99% deviation and triggered an update every single minute — regardless of whether prices actually moved. Use index 2 (lastValue) for the price and index 1 (lastBlockTimestamp) for the staleness check. Block timestamp is the right reference for staleness because it reflects when the update actually landed on-chain. Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

author: ianhe8x
message: Add regression tests for skip-slot fork handling in unfinalized blocks Covers: forks behind missed slots, rebuilding the parent chain across real and skipped slots, and rolling back when a backfilled or new block doesn't connect to the expected parent.

author: ianhe8x
message: Only treat SLOT_SKIPPED as a confirmed skipped slot BLOCK_NOT_AVAILABLE and LONG_TERM_STORAGE_SLOT_SKIPPED don't reliably mean a slot was skipped (the former can be a transient node-lag signal, the latter an archival backfill gap), so silently converting them to BlockUnavailableError risked masking real blocks instead of just crashing on them.

author: folknor
message: Commit cached add transaction state before persisting it (#4783) `Cache::add_order` populated every index, called `database.add_order`, then wrote the canonical cell, so a persistence failure left the order indexed but absent from `orders`. `add_position_id` split the same way internally, persisting between the forward mapping and its reverse indexes, and `add_position_inner` inherited that through its nested call with two further fallible writes between the index families. Split `add_position_id` into a memory half and a persistence half so both callers commit the whole operation, canonical cell included, before any database call. Splitting at the public boundary alone would leave a database write inside their memory transaction. The position path keeps its three writes fail-fast and in order, and its OMS entry no longer goes through `Cache::add`: the general insert moves into the commit phase, with key validation and serialization hoisted ahead of any mutation. Align `replace_order` with `update_order` on ordering by preflighting the venue order ID ownership check and committing the cell before refreshing. It still propagates a persistence error rather than logging it, because callers use that signal. The settlement registration-failure test asserted the old shape, so its stale-index expectations are inverted; what it pins otherwise is unchanged. Coded by an LLM.

author: carlotestor
message: build(go): trampoline async cores so Promise.all fans out like the C#/Java ports (#29647) * build(go): emit buffered (capacity 1) channels for async exchange cores ast-transpiler emits every async Go method as an unbuffered result channel: ch := make(chan any) go func() any { defer close(ch) defer ReturnPanicError(ch) ... ch <- value }() return ch The channel carries exactly one value (a resolved promise) and is closed immediately after, so the unbuffered form buys nothing: it only forces the producing goroutine to block on `ch <-` until a receiver shows up. Give those channels capacity 1 (`make(chan any, 1)`) at write time in build/goTranspiler.ts, so the goroutine can deposit its single value and exit without a rendezvous. Why it is safe: - one-shot promise semantics: exactly one send, then close(ch) - the generated typed wrappers receive immediately (`res := <-this.Core.FetchTicker(...)`), so no consumer behaviour changes - a caller that abandons the channel (early return, select-with-timeout, cancelled errgroup) no longer leaks a goroutine parked forever on the send - ReturnPanicError(ch) can deliver its panic message without a live receiver - it is the precondition for later inlining the body instead of nesting a goroutine, because a fill-before-return core cannot self-deadlock at cap 1 Implemented as a post-process in formatGoSource() (plus the one fs.writeFileSync that bypasses it, the prediction base), so it covers every Go emitter path — exchange cores, base methods, pro/, prediction/ and the transpiled base tests — without forking ast-transpiler. The regex is anchored on the `defer close(ch)` + `defer [pkg.]ReturnPanicError(ch)` goroutine header, only rewrites the single-type-argument `make(chan T)` form, and is idempotent (an already-buffered make has a capacity argument and no longer matches). Verified locally: - tsx build/goTranspiler.ts bit2c --force -> 11/11 cores buffered, 0 unbuffered - tsx build/goTranspiler.ts bitopro --ws --force -> 6/6 pro cores buffered - exchange_generated.go regenerated: 264 changed lines, all `make(chan any)` -> `make(chan any, 1)`, no other drift - re-running the same transpile is byte-identical (md5) and produces no `make(chan any, 1, 1)` - applied the identical transform to the whole generated tree (4886 sites in 238 files) to simulate a full regen, then: go build -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction -> OK go build -C go ./tests/main.go -> OK go vet -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction ./tests/base -> clean gofmt -l go/v4 -> same 4 pre-existing files as on unmodified master - tsc --noEmit clean; eslint clean - generated go/ dumps discarded; this commit touches build/goTranspiler.ts only Hand-written base channels (throttler task channels, Future, promiseAll's panicChan, WS subscription channels, exchange_helpers) are untouched: they do not match the async-core header and none of them is generated anyway. * build(go): run async exchange cores inline instead of in a nested goroutine Follow-up to the buffered-channel change in this PR. Now that every async core hands back a capacity-1 channel, the goroutine it spawns is dead weight: the body can fill the channel in place and return it already resolved. func (this *Bit2cCore) FetchBalance(...) <-chan any { -> (out <-chan any) { ch := make(chan any, 1) ch := make(chan any, 1) go func() any { out = ch defer close(ch) defer close(ch) defer ReturnPanicError(ch) defer ReturnPanicError(ch) ... ... ch <- value ch <- value return nil return ch }() return ch } That removes one goroutine per call across ~4.8k methods and makes a failing request show the caller in its stack trace instead of a detached `go func`. Why the result has to be named: `defer ReturnPanicError(ch)` recovers the panic, so on the error path the function returns *normally*. With an unnamed result Go then hands back the zero value of `<-chan any` - a nil channel - and every caller blocks on it forever. Assigning `out = ch` before the defers and rewriting the core-level `return nil` into `return ch` keeps the channel reachable on both paths. Naming a result does not change the method's type, so the generated wrappers and the typed interfaces are untouched (`go build` covers this). The rewrite is conservative - a core that is not provably safe keeps its goroutine, which is still correct code. 4796 of 4884 cores flatten; the 88 skipped ones break down as: - 46 fire-and-forget cores (`Authenticate`, `WatchSpotPublic`, `WatchSwapPublic`). A bare statement call that drops the result channel is how a floating JS promise transpiles. Those call sites only work because the call returns before the work is done: inline, `pro/mexc.go`'s unwatch methods would block on a websocket message the same method is meant to trigger, and `HandleUnsubscriptions` would never be reached. - 20 cores that send from inside a nested func literal. There `return nil` leaves only the closure, so the core can reach a second send - which on a capacity-1 channel would block the caller. `Fetch2` (every REST request) is one of these, so it deliberately keeps its goroutine. - 22 cores whose body contains a block comment, where the brace scan that classifies nesting cannot be trusted. Dropping the trailing `return ch` matters: the body already ends in a terminating statement (the `go func() any` it came from had to, to compile), so emitting the outer one as well leaves unreachable code, which `go vet` reports as an error. Caught by vet on the first full-tree run. Applied through the same write-time funnel as the buffering, so it covers every Go emitter path - exchange cores, base methods, pro/, prediction/ and the transpiled base tests - without forking ast-transpiler. Verified locally: - tsx build/goTranspiler.ts bit2c --force -> cores emit the flat shape - tsx build/goTranspiler.ts bitopro --ws --force -> same for pro/ (ccxt.-qualified helper) - tsx build/goTranspiler.ts polymarket --prediction --force -> same for prediction/ - the prediction base write bypasses formatGoSource and gofmt; its 39 space-indented cores flatten too, and go build ./v4 stays green - applied the transform to the whole generated tree (240 of 712 files) to simulate a full regen, then: go build -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction -> OK go build -C go ./tests/main.go -> OK go vet -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction ./tests/base -> clean gofmt -l go/v4 -> empty - re-running the transform over the tree changes 0 of 712 files (idempotent) - the transform's output is byte-identical (md5) to what the real transpiler writes for bit2c.go and exchange_generated.go - runtime check against the real helpers in go/v4: flattened cores return the value on the happy path and the `panic:...` string on the panic path, nested cores propagate, and the rejected unnamed-result variant deadlocks - which is what the named result is there to prevent - tsc --noEmit clean; eslint clean - generated go/ dumps discarded; this commit touches build/goTranspiler.ts only Behaviour change worth calling out: cores no longer return before their work is done, so callers that fired several off and awaited them afterwards now run them sequentially. `promiseAll` still returns correct results (each task channel is already filled and closed when it reads it), and the websocket read loop and the throttler both drive their own goroutines, so blocking the caller is safe there. * build(go): flatten the remaining 88 async cores, fix their call sites Completes the flattening started in the previous commit: 4884 of 4884 async cores (100%) now run their body inline and hand back a filled capacity-1 channel. The 88 that kept their goroutine did so for three reasons; each is fixed at the source rather than skipped. 1. Sends from inside a try/catch shim (20 cores, incl. Fetch2) ast-transpiler turns `try { … } catch (e) { … }` into an immediately-invoked func literal, and a `return` inside the try leaves only that literal. In JS the same `return` leaves the whole async function, so the Go port keeps running, reaches a second `ch <-`, and on a capacity-1 channel that second send would block the caller forever. The flattener now threads a `chSent` flag through those cores and returns the moment the shim produced a value: for … { for … { { { func(this *X) (ret_ any) { func(this *X) (ret_ any) { ch <- response ch <- response chSent = true return nil return nil }(this) }(this) } if chSent { } return ch } } } That is also a real bug fix independent of this PR. With `maxRetries` at its default 3 the loop kept going after a *successful* call, so one SafeDeterministicCall / FetchRestOrderBookSafe issued up to three requests; the caller only ever saw the first value, which is why nobody noticed. Measured against the generated tree, driving a real BinanceCore at a local server: Fetch2, maxRetriesOnFailure=3, success first try before: 2 requests after: 1 request 2. Fire-and-forget cores (46: Authenticate, WatchSpotPublic, WatchSwapPublic) The previous commit assumed a bare statement call dropping the result channel needed the goroutine. Auditing all 196 call sites showed only 9 are actually affected, all of them `pro/mexc.go` unWatch methods, and that the 5 Authenticate sites named in that commit message are *synchronous void* functions the transform never touched. The 9 are fixed where the bug actually is — the TypeScript: this.watchSwapPublic (channel, messageHash, requestParams, params); -> this.spawn (this.watchSwapPublic, channel, messageHash, requestParams, params); `spawn` is the existing fire-and-forget helper (Exchange.ts, already used by mexc.ts itself) and it transpiles to `this.Spawn(this.WatchSwapPublic, …)` in Go. Doing it in TypeScript also repairs the other ports, where the floating promise is worse than in Go: in Python a bare `self.watch_swap_public(...)` builds a coroutine that is never awaited, so the unsubscribe request is never sent at all. Rewriting call sites in Go instead was tried and rejected — `Spawn` reflects into the callee and would panic on the void `bitopro`/`weex` Authenticate. 3. Block comments in the body (22 cores) The brace scan bailed out on `/* … */` because a comment can hide braces. It now tracks the open-comment state across lines instead, which is all that was needed; these bodies are ordinary single-send cores. The safety gates that remain are the ones that describe shapes the rewrite genuinely does not model: an unbalanced parse, a core-level return that is not `return nil`, a body that already uses the identifier `out` or `chSent`, and a multi-line send (none exist today, but a `ch <- map[string]any{` spanning lines would put the flag assignment in the wrong place). Verified: - census over a full regenerated tree: 4884 cores, 4884 flat, 0 nested. The only `go func() any` left in go/ are 3 in the hand-written exchange.go, which the transpiler never writes - go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction, go build ./tests/main.go -> OK - go vet ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction ./tests/base -> clean - gofmt -l go/v4 go/tests -> only prediction/exchange_wrapper_structs.go, which is already unformatted on master and untouched here - go test ./v4/... -> ok (lmtsprobe fails identically at HEAD, unrelated) - re-running the transform over the tree changes 0 of 712 files (idempotent) - output is byte-identical (md5) to what the real transpiler writes for all three emitter paths: bit2c + exchange_generated (REST), mexc + bitopro (--ws), myriad + exchange_prediction (--prediction, the write that bypasses gofmt) - runtime, against the real go/v4 through a local server: happy path, one request per call, the retry loop stopping on success, panic path returning a non-nil channel with the error, channel already filled on return, closed after one value, 200 sequential calls, 16 concurrent callers, no goroutine growth over 300 calls - tsc --noEmit and eslint clean - generated go/ discarded; this commit touches build/goTranspiler.ts and ts/src/pro/mexc.ts only. CI regenerates the ports. Behaviour change worth repeating from the previous commit: cores no longer return before their work is done, so callers that fired several off and awaited them afterwards now run them sequentially. promiseAll still returns correct results (each task channel is already filled and closed when it reads it), and the websocket read loop and the throttler drive their own goroutines. * go: accept Future tasks in promiseAll ast-transpiler#64 emits a deferred async call -- one that is stored, or pushed into an array, and awaited later -- as `this.Spawn(this.Method, args...).Await()` so a flat core still fans out concurrently instead of running to completion at the point of evaluation. That shape already works here: `Future.Await()` returns a `<-chan any`, so the existing `task.(<-chan any)` assertion holds and `promiseAll` needs nothing new for the generated code. Verified against a harness replicating the real Spawn/Future/promiseAll contracts: promiseAll([]any{ Spawn(a).Await(), Spawn(b).Await() }) -> [a b] What is fixed here is the neighbouring foot-gun. A bare `*Future` -- a Spawn result handed to promiseAll without `.Await()`, which is what a hand-written call site or a future emit tweak would most naturally produce -- fell into the "not a channel" branch and was recorded as **nil**, silently losing the value with no panic and no error: promiseAll([]any{ Spawn(a), Spawn(b) }) -> [<nil> <nil>] The type switch adds the `*Future` case (and `chan any` alongside `<-chan any`) and keeps the historical nil for anything genuinely not awaitable, so no existing behaviour changes. go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction -> exit 0 go vet ./v4 ./v4/pro -> exit 0 gofmt -l -> clean harness under -race -> clean * chore(build): pin ast-transpiler to merged upstream master ccxt/ast-transpiler#64 is merged, so track master HEAD (17e855356cc0726af615d0ac9b051bedeeb33982) instead of the pre-merge branch commit. The lock entry is hand-rewritten to git+https:// because npm normalizes github deps to git+ssh://, which GitHub Actions runners cannot fetch; `npm install` silently reverts that rewrite, `npm ci` preserves it. * build(go): let ast-transpiler own the flat async core, keep the multi-send guard The pinned ast-transpiler now emits every async core flat, on a capacity-1 channel, with a named result, so the CCXT-side buffer and flatten passes are dead weight: their gate (a nested `go func() any {`) no longer appears in any generated file, which made them silent no-ops. Drop both. What the emitter does not do is stop a core after its first send. A `return` inside a transpiled `try` block only leaves the synthetic closure, so a retry loop keeps going and sends again. That used to park a goroutine nobody read; on a flat core with a capacity-1 channel the second send blocks the caller instead, so the same shape now deadlocks (measured with the emitted shape: caller blocked, two requests issued). Keep that part as guardMultiSendCores(), which threads a chSent flag through the four base methods that have it — Fetch2, FetchWebEndpoint, SafeDeterministicCall, FetchRestOrderBookSafe — and leaves the other 299 cores byte-identical. The guard also fixes the retry bug those loops have today: with maxRetries at its default 3 the loop re-issued a successful request up to three times and the caller only ever saw the first value. * fix(go): add Spawn on testMainClass for deferred async emit ast-transpiler#64 wraps deferred async this.X() as this.Spawn(this.Method, args...).Await(). The live-test harness class is not an Exchange, so CI's `go build ./tests/main.go` failed with `this.Spawn undefined` at 7 sites in tests.go. Mirror BaseExchange.Spawn on testMainClass in a hand-written sibling file so regen of tests.go still compiles. Verified: npx tsx build/goTranspiler.ts --tests --force emits the 7 Spawn sites CI reported; go build ./tests/main.go, ./v4, ./v4/pro, ./v4/prediction all exit 0. Generated test dumps not committed (CI regenerates). * fix(go): run module-scope async fan-out concurrently too The Spawn wrap that keeps a deferred async call from serializing a later Promise.all was gated on the callee being a method on `this`. The transpiled test harness is written as module-scope `async function`s, so its fan-outs fell through the gate and stayed serial: var withoutSymbol any = TestWatchTickersHelper(exchange, props, nil) var withSymbol any = TestWatchTickersHelper(exchange, props, []any{symbol}) retRes114 := (<-promiseAll([]any{withSymbol, withoutSymbol})) A flat core runs inline, so each call completed before the next one started. tests.go:2434 was the clearest proof: in ONE array literal the `this.` element was wrapped and its module-scope sibling was not. ccxt/ast-transpiler#66 accepts a bare identifier callee that resolves to an async FunctionDeclaration and emits the package-level twin `Spawn(Helper, args...).Await()` — a free function has no receiver. Add that Spawn to the generated tests package; testMainClass.Spawn now delegates to it instead of duplicating the body. Six sites become concurrent: test.watchTickers, test.watchBidsAsks (two 15s watch loops that were running end to end) and test.fetchTickers, x2 each. Measured with a Go timing harness on the real regenerated code, two ~100ms deferred calls joined by Promise.all: 200ms serial -> 100ms concurrent, the two Await() lines taking 0ms (Await never blocks). Panics still surface: the panicking branch carries its "panic:..." string and the healthy sibling still resolves. go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction and go build -C go ./tests/main.go both exit 0. The pin is a fork SHA because ast-transpiler#66 is not merged yet; repoint it at ccxt/ast-transpiler master once it lands. * chore(build): pin ast-transpiler to merged upstream master ccxt/ast-transpiler#66 (free-function Spawn wrap) is merged, so the temporary fork pin is no longer needed. package.json goes back to github:ccxt/ast-transpiler#master and the lock resolves to current master (9bb28b1, which has 0d0589d = the #66 merge as an ancestor). The lock entry is hand-rewritten to git+https:// because npm hosted-git-info normalises every github.com git dep to git+ssh://, and GHA runners have no SSH key even for public repos. Note for reviewers: a plain `npm install` silently reverts that scheme back to ssh -- `npm ci` preserves it. Verified CI-safe by installing the pinned lock with GIT_SSH_COMMAND=/bin/false. * fix(go): recover panics in Spawn so request tests do not kill the process `npm run request-go` died with panic: panic:... [NotSupported]::[grvt signIn() is not supported ccxt.(*BaseExchange).Spawn.func1() go/v4/exchange.go:2174 tests/base.Spawn.func1() go/tests/base/test.spawn.go:30 exit status 2 Now that async cores run flat (inline on the caller goroutine), a core recovers its own body panic into its channel via `defer ReturnPanicError(ch)` and the awaiting site re-panics it through PanicOnError. When that awaiting site is Spawn, the re-panic lands on Spawn s own goroutine -- the root of its stack, with no caller left to recover it -- so it took the whole test binary down. Previously the nested goroutine inside each core absorbed this. Recover in both Spawn bodies and hand the failure to waiters exactly as a flattened core would: resolve the Future with the same "panic:..." string that IsError / CreateReturnError / PanicOnError already understand, so wrappers keep turning it into (T, error) instead of hanging. "break" (the transpiler loop marker) resolves nil, mirroring ReturnPanicError. ReturnPanicError itself is deliberately untouched: legacy unbuffered cores rely on its send blocking. The blind `.(<-chan any)` assert was a second process-killer -- it panics when CallDynamically returns nil for a void callee -- so it becomes a type switch, with nil-channel guards so a typed-nil channel resolves instead of blocking a waiter forever. Verified: full `--requestTests` suite passes, 4431 static request tests, exit 0, zero Spawn.func1 frames (it previously died on grvt signIn). A harness against the real ccxt and tests/base packages confirms, for both Spawn twins, that an escaping panic now leaves the process alive with the panic string delivered to the waiter, while the pre-fix body dies with exit=2; happy path, error/Reject, void/nil callee, concurrency and promiseAll interop all still behave. * fix(go): keep virtual base methods dispatching through callInternal The free-function/deferred Spawn wrap from ast-transpiler#66 also fired on virtual base methods, and there it is wrong. `this.Spawn(this.SignIn).Await()` freezes a method value bound to the embedded *BaseExchange*, so the venue override is never reached: Promise.all ([ this.loadMarkets (), this.signIn () ]) (Exchange.ts:8876) emitted `this.Spawn(this.SignIn).Await()` instead of the previous `<-this.callInternal("signIn")`, so grvt.signIn() ran BaseExchange.SignIn and panicked `NotSupported: grvt signIn() is not supported yet`. Go has no virtual dispatch on `this` -- that is exactly what the callInternal / DerivedExchange rewrites in this file exist for -- and `signIn` is not on IDerivedExchange, so it has to stay on the callInternal path. Undo the wrap for VIRTUAL_BASE_METHODS only, in both the main and prediction base passes, before those rewrites run. Non-virtual deferred calls (this.LoadMarkets, this.SafeDeterministicCall) keep the concurrent Spawn wrap, so the #66 fan-out is preserved where it is safe. Verified on the regenerated base: LoadMarketsAndSignIn emits `promiseAll([]any{this.Spawn(this.LoadMarkets).Await(), <-this.callInternal("signIn")})`, gofmt clean, `go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction` -> 0, and `--requestTests` now reports 4431 passed with 0 TEST_FAILURE and 0 NotSupported (previously 1 failure on grvt signIn). tsc --noEmit -> 0. * build(go): adapt to the trampoline async emit and drop the Spawn workarounds ast-transpiler now emits async cores as TRAMPOLINES (ccxt/ast-transpiler#67): the core allocates the cap-1 channel, launches the body on its own goroutine and returns the channel immediately, so every async call is a hot handle exactly like a C# Task or a Java CompletableFuture. func (this *Bit2cCore) FetchBalance(...) <-chan any { ch := make(chan any, 1) go func() any { defer close(ch) defer ReturnPanicError(ch) ... ch <- value return nil }() return ch } Consequences on the CCXT side: - guardMultiSendCores is KEPT and retargeted at the new shape. The multi-send problem it fixes is unchanged: `try { ... return x } catch {}` inside a retry loop is emulated with an immediately-invoked closure, so the `return` leaves only the closure, the loop keeps going and a second `ch <-` has nowhere to go on a cap-1 channel. maxRetries defaults to 3, so up to three sends are possible where the buffer absorbs one. The prologue matcher now expects `go func() any {` instead of `out = ch`, and knows the two defers sit one level deeper; the scan excludes the trampoline's own `}()` / `return ch` tail so func-literal depths still line up; and the early return it injects is `return nil` (leaving the body goroutine), not `return ch`. It also still fixes the real bug where SafeDeterministicCall and FetchRestOrderBookSafe re-issue a successful request up to three times. - The two passes that un-wrapped `this.Spawn(this.Method, ...).Await()` back into callInternal for virtual base methods are DELETED. They existed because the emitter wrapped deferred calls in Spawn, freezing a method value bound to the embedded *BaseExchange and losing the venue override (grvt.signIn hit the base stub and panicked NotSupported). The emitter produces no such wrap any more, so `<-this.callInternal("signIn")` is emitted directly again and virtual dispatch is correct by construction. - go/tests/base/test.spawn.go is removed: it was added only to give the transpiled test harness a Spawn for module-scope async helpers. Those helpers are trampolines now, so nothing references it -- `go build -C go ./tests/main.go` passes without it. `exchange.Spawn` in test.unWatchPositions.go is BaseExchange.Spawn and is unaffected. Kept deliberately: - BaseExchange.Spawn and its panic recover: real TypeScript `this.spawn (...)` calls still exist (mexc unWatch, myriad pong, Exchange.delay) and still map to it. The spawned goroutine is the root of its own stack, so an escaping panic still kills the process without the recover. Comment updated. - promiseAll's *Future case, for those same un-awaited spawn results. - ts/src/pro/mexc.ts `this.spawn (this.watchSpotPublic, ...)`: a genuine fire-and-forget unWatch in the TypeScript source, not an emit artifact. package.json/lock pin ast-transpiler at carlotestor/ast-transpiler@73af0ba (ccxt/ast-transpiler#67) until that PR merges; repoint to github:ccxt/ast-transpiler#master afterwards. Lock rewritten to git+https so CI needs no SSH key: verified with `GIT_SSH_COMMAND=/bin/false npm ci`. Verified: npm run force-transpileGO exits 0; no `(out <-chan` or `out = ch` anywhere in the regenerated tree; chSent guards present on Fetch2, FetchWebEndpoint, SafeDeterministicCall and FetchRestOrderBookSafe; `go build -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction`, `go build -C go ./tests/main.go` and `go vet` all exit 0. Runtime harness on go1.25.5: two 100ms trampoline cores stored in variables and joined with promiseAll finish in 100ms (the previous flat emit took 200ms), 2000 abandoned trampolines leak 0 goroutines, and a panicking body is delivered to the waiter as a "panic:..." string on a non-nil channel with the process surviving. * build(go): adapt to the sibling-body trampoline emit ast-transpiler#67 now emits an async core as an explicit trampoline + BODY pair instead of wrapping the body in an anonymous goroutine inside the core's own signature (ccxt/ast-transpiler@6c73e87): func (this *Bit2cCore) FetchBalance(optionalArgs ...any) <-chan any { ch := make(chan any, 1) go this.fetchBalanceBody(ch, optionalArgs...) return ch } func (this *Bit2cCore) fetchBalanceBody(ch chan any, optionalArgs ...any) any { defer close(ch) defer ReturnPanicError(ch) ... ch <- value return nil } Semantics are unchanged from the previous commit -- cap-1 channel, recover on the goroutine that can panic, unnamed `<-chan any` result, every call already a hot handle -- so nothing about the Spawn removal or the dropped named `out` is revisited here. Two things on this side had to follow the new shape. - guardMultiSendCores is KEPT and retargeted a second time. The bug it fixes is the same: `try { ... return x } catch {}` inside a retry loop is emulated with an immediately-invoked closure, so the `return` leaves only the closure, the loop keeps going, and a second `ch <-` has nowhere to go on a cap-1 channel. What changed is only where the core is recognised: the scanned unit is now the BODY, matched by `func …(ch chan any, …) any {` immediately followed by the two defers, and the body is flat, so the make/`go func`/tail bookkeeping is gone along with GO_CORE_MAKE, GO_CORE_GO, GO_CORE_GO_END and GO_CORE_RETURN_CH. The public trampoline is three statements and can never multi-send, so it is not scanned at all. The injected early return is still `return nil`, which now leaves the body method rather than a closure; `defer close(ch)` still runs. Guards still land on Fetch2, FetchWebEndpoint, SafeDeterministicCall, FetchRestOrderBookSafe and the four transpiled test helpers -- 12 files, same set as before. - The regex that drops the transpiled *Exchange copy of loadOrderBook (it is hand-written in exchange.go, using WS cache primitives the transpiler cannot emit) cut to the next `func (this *Exchange)`. That is now the method's own lowercase body, so the cut stopped one function early and left `loadOrderBookBody` behind -- untranspilable and uncompilable (`stored.Cache undefined`, `tries++` on any). It now cuts to the next EXPORTED method, taking the orphaned body with it. The body is emitted unexported on purpose, so it stays off the generated ICoreExchange/IDerivedExchange interfaces and off the typed `*_wrapper.go` facades: `grep -c Body go/v4/exchange_interface.go` finds only the unrelated `responseBody` parameter, no `*_wrapper.go` mentions a Body method at all, and wrappers still read `res := <-this.Core.FetchBalance(...)`. package.json/lock pin ast-transpiler at carlotestor/ast-transpiler@6c73e87 (ccxt/ast-transpiler#67) until that PR merges; repoint to github:ccxt/ast-transpiler#master afterwards. Lock rewritten to git+https so CI needs no SSH key: verified with `GIT_SSH_COMMAND=/bin/false npm ci`. Verified: npm run force-transpileGO exits 0; the regenerated tree has 4877 `go this.<method>Body(ch, …)` handoffs plus 67 package-level ones, zero `go func() any {` envelopes outside hand-written exchange.go, and zero `(out <-chan` / `out = ch`; `go build -C go ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction`, `go build -C go ./tests/main.go` and `go vet` all exit 0. Runtime harness on go1.25.5: two 100ms trampoline cores stored in variables and joined with promiseAll finish in 100ms with no call-site Spawn, 2000 abandoned trampolines leak 0 goroutines, and a panicking body is delivered to the waiter as a "panic:kaboom" string on a non-nil channel with the process surviving. * go: fix stale trampoline sketch in build/goTranspiler.ts comment The emitter produces a trampoline plus an unexported sibling body method, not a nested go func() any envelope. Comment-only. * build: bump ast-transpiler pin to 44ce313 (doc-comment fix, no emit change) * build: repin ast-transpiler to ccxt/ast-transpiler#master (#67 merged) ast-transpiler PR ccxt/ast-transpiler#67 (go: async cores become trampolines handing work to a sibling *Body goroutine) is MERGED. Drop the temporary carlotestor fork pin and go back to upstream: package.json: github:ccxt/ast-transpiler#master lock resolved: git+https://github.com/ccxt/ast-transpiler.git#c1ede757 c1ede7579862813309cb9a6d600b50b4b44a1069 is both the merge commit of #67 and current ccxt/ast-transpiler master HEAD. The lock keeps git+https (hand-edited): npm's hosted-git-info always writes git+ssh for github deps, which GHA runners cannot fetch.

author: carlotestor
message: fix(kraken): single-flight websockets token authenticate (refs #29393) (#29996) * fix(kraken): single-flight websockets token authenticate (refs #29393) authenticate () re-checks a staleness gate and then awaits privatePostGetWebSocketsToken (), so N concurrent watchPrivate () calls on a cold instance all pass the gate and each burn a rate-limited private REST call to mint a separate token. Elect a single leader through the client's own future registry: client.futures is the flight map, the leader mints `const future = client.future (messageHash)` BEFORE the first await, and the flight is settled exclusively through client.resolve () / client.reject () - both of which delete the registry entry themselves, so there is no hand-rolled delete and no flag parked in client.subscriptions. Because the leader always holds a waiter, reject () can never park an error in client.rejections[] where it would poison the first waiter of the next retry flight. The trailing `await future` rethrows the leader's own failure instead of a bare `throw e`, which also guarantees the rejection is always consumed. Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: same REST call, same 'authenticated' subscription cache write with the venue expires/start stamps, and the empty-token AuthenticationError guard stays inside the try so it routes through client.reject () to every waiter. The flight hash 'authenticateFlight' is parked on the client for urls['api']['ws']['private'] (wss://ws-auth.kraken.com), which authenticate () is the only consumer of - every watch* uses privateV2 / publicV2 - so it cannot collide with a real messageHash. Verified: npm run tsBuild (exit 0); eslint on both touched files (clean); the native TS wiring test ts/src/pro/test/base/ test.singleFlightWiring.kraken.ts passes (5 concurrent authenticates => exactly 1 fetch, client.futures / pendingResults / rejections all empty afterwards, solo-leader rejection produces no unhandled rejection); negative control neutering the early-return guard fails with 5 fetches; scoped `tsx build/transpileWS.ts kraken --force` emits Python/PHP without error. * test(kraken): drop client.pendingResults reads (field removed upstream) client.pendingResults was deleted from ts/src/base/ws/Client.ts upstream, so residueCount () now counts client.rejections only and the assert messages no longer name the removed field. Also corrects testKrakenAuthenticateWaiterAlwaysSettles (): close () walks every entry of exchange.clients, including the never-dialed private client that carries the flight, so it rejects the flight future. Both the leader and the waiter must observe ExchangeClosedByUser instead of completing with the held-open token. Handlers are now attached up front so the rejection is never unhandled, matching the shared dispatcher's aster/binance/bingx shape.

author: carlotestor
message: fix(bitstamp): single-flight websocket token authenticate (refs #29393) (#29994) * fix(bitstamp): single-flight websocket token authenticate (refs #29393) bitstamp authenticate () did an unguarded check-then-fetch: it read the staleness stamp, awaited privatePostWebsocketsToken (), and only then wrote the cache. Every concurrent subscribePrivate () caller on a cold instance passed the staleness check and minted its own websocket token. The tokens are short lived (valid_sec is 60), so this burns the private endpoint and only the last write survives - earlier callers can end up subscribing with a userId/token pair that has already been replaced. Wraps the existing fetch in an inlined single-flight leader election on a never-dialed 'authenticationFlights' client, using the same shape as the aster/binance/bingx work in PR #29992: const messageHash = 'authenticateFlight'; const client = this.client ('authenticationFlights'); if (messageHash in client.futures) { await client.future (messageHash); return; } const future = client.future (messageHash); try { ...fetch + cache write...; client.resolve (sessionToken, messageHash); } catch (e) { client.reject (e, messageHash); } await future; The flight is registered in client.futures and settled exclusively through client.resolve / client.reject, which delete the entry themselves under the client's own lock - no `client.subscriptions` flag and no hand-rolled `delete client.futures[...]`, both of which are unlocked read-modify-writes against a mutex-guarded map once transpiled to the Go/PHP/C# ports. The leader mints its future BEFORE the first await, so client.reject always has a waiter and never parks the error in client.rejections; a parked rejection would otherwise be consumed by the first waiter of the next retry flight. The trailing `await future` (instead of an explicit `throw e`) rethrows to the leader and marks the promise handled, so a solo leader's failure is never an unhandled rejection. Also converts the silent `if (sessionToken !== undefined)` guard into an explicit AuthenticationError before any cache write. On master a hollow 200 cached nothing AND threw nothing, so expiresIn stayed stale and every caller proceeded to subscribe with an empty auth field. The throw stays inside the try, so it routes through client.reject: the cache is untouched, every waiter observes the error and the next caller re-leads. The fetch, the cached fields (expiresIn, userId, wsSessionToken) and the staleness gate are otherwise unchanged. Adds ts/src/pro/test/base/test.singleFlightWiring.bitstamp.ts, a native TS test (intentionally not wired into tests.init - the logic is inlined in authenticate (), so nothing else guards it). Verified: npm run tsBuild exits 0; eslint clean on both touched files; the wiring test passes - 4 concurrent authenticates produce exactly 1 fetch and leave client.futures / pendingResults / rejections empty, plus the empty-token and solo-leader rejection cases; negative control neutering the `messageHash in client.futures` early return makes it fail with 4 fetches; scoped `transpileWS.ts bitstamp --force` emits python/php/go without error. Refs #29393 Refs #29992 * test(bitstamp): drop client.pendingResults reads (field removed upstream)

message: fix(lbank): single-flight subscribeKey authenticate (refs #29393) (#29993) * fix(lbank): single-flight subscribeKey authenticate (refs #29393) lbank's pro authenticate() did an unguarded check-then-fetch in BOTH of its branches, and the code said so itself: the method opened with "when we implement more private streams, we need to refactor the authentication to be concurrent-safe and respect the same authentication token" (ts/src/pro/lbank.ts:973-974 on master). Cold path (ts/src/pro/lbank.ts:979-993 on master): every caller read client.subscriptions['authenticated'] === undefined, then awaited its own spotPrivatePostSubscribeGetKey, then wrote the bucket. N concurrent watchOrders()/watchBalance() calls on a cold instance minted N subscribeKeys; last write won and the earlier keys were orphaned. Expired path (ts/src/pro/lbank.ts:995-1009 on master): every caller read the same stale expires, then awaited its own spotPrivatePostSubscribeRefreshKey. N concurrent callers past the 55 minute mark each POSTed a refresh for the same key. Both are reachable from user code: watchOrders (:564) and watchBalance (:731) both call authenticate() and both are commonly started together. Fix: the inlined single-flight leader election from #29992. lbank already has a `client` local bound to its live ws url and its credential already lives on that client's subscriptions map, so the flight is parked on that same client under the namespaced key 'authenticateFlight' rather than on a dummy never-dialed client - 'authenticateFlight' is provably not one of lbank's messageHashes. The flight wraps the whole if/else, so the refresh is single-flighted too. Waiters read client.subscriptions['authenticated']['key'] fresh after waking. Because the flight rides a genuinely dialed client, the WsClient.close() settlement change from #29992 is not needed here: a real client already fires the onClose -> reset -> reject chain for its pending futures. checkRequiredCredentials() is hoisted from inside the cold branch to the top of the method so a credential-less caller throws before registering a flight nobody would settle. No behaviour change for valid callers. The existing ExchangeError guards for result !== true / result !== 'true' are unchanged; they now land inside the try and correctly reject the flight so waiters throw and the next caller re-leads. Verified: npm run tsBuild (exit 0), single-file eslint (exit 0), npm run test-base-ws-ts ("base WS tests passed!"), and the new ts/src/pro/test/base/test.singleFlightWiring.lbank.ts, which fails on master (5 get_key POSTs) and passes with the fix (1). Refs #29393 Refs #29992 * fix(lbank): settle the authenticate flight through client.futures Follow-up to eeb4a87 on the same fix. The previous revision parked the single-flight registration flag in client.subscriptions['authenticateFlight'] and hand-rolled the settlement, reaching into client.futures to delete the entry and calling future.resolve () / future.reject () directly. That works, but it duplicates logic the base Client already owns and it only minted the shared future lazily in the first waiter, so the leader's own rejection had no handler attached on the solo path. This revision moves the flight onto the registry the base class already treats as a dedup map: - the flight is registered with const future = client.future (messageHash) BEFORE the first fetch, so client.reject () always has a waiter and never parks the error in client.rejections[] - a parked rejection would poison the FIRST waiter of the next retry flight - settlement goes exclusively through client.resolve () / client.reject (), which delete the futures entry themselves (Client.ts:167-170, :186-189), so there is no manual delete and no flag left in client.subscriptions - the method ends in await future instead of throw e: that single await both rethrows the failure to the leader and attaches the handler that keeps an alone leader from crashing the process on an unhandled rejection The client key is unchanged - the flight still rides this exchange's own ws client at urls['api']['ws'], the same one that carries subscriptions['authenticated'], under a key that is not one of its messageHashes. Both REST branches (spotPrivatePostSubscribeGetKey on a cold cache, spotPrivatePostSubscribeRefreshKey past the expiry) stay inside the one try, so the one flight covers both. The checkRequiredCredentials () guard still runs before the flight is registered, so a credential-less caller throws immediately instead of parking a flight nobody would settle. Also rewords the leading comment to avoid a bare "await" inside it. The PHP async emitter rewrites /\sawait\s+([^;]+);/ across newlines (build/transpile.ts:708), so the word "await" in a comment swallowed everything up to the next semicolon and emitted `$this->check_required_credentials());` - php -l failed with "Unclosed '{' on line 1027 does not match ')'". Reworded, php -l and the full php/pro/test/custom/syntax.php suite are clean again. Verification (ts/src/pro only; generated trees reverted before commit): - npx tsc --noEmit: exit 0, 0 errors - npm run eslint ts/src/pro/lbank.ts + the wiring test: exit 0, clean - ts/src/pro/test/base/test.singleFlightWiring.lbank.ts: all 6 cases pass - negative control: neutering the early-return guard to if (false) makes the cold case report 5 subscribe/get_key POSTs instead of 1 - scoped transpile: python/php/go emit without error; py_compile OK, php -l OK, go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction exit 0 * test(lbank): drop client.pendingResults reads (field removed upstream)

author: carlotestor
message: refactor(pro): inline the ws auth single-flight logic into authenticate() (#29992) * refactor(base): inline singleFlightAcquire onto binance/aster/bingx the ws auth single-flight primitives from #29903 were added to the Exchange base with hand-written mirrors in all six language ports, for three exchanges that use them. that put a non-unified, ws-only concern on the base class of every exchange and forced six hand-maintained copies to stay in lockstep. the four methods now live on the three exchanges that wire them, so the base class and every port mirror lose the mapping entirely. - authenticate() call sites are byte-identical to master: they still call this.singleFlightAcquire / singleFlightResolve / singleFlightReject, and the fetch/cache/keepalive bodies are untouched - storage moves to a never-dialed this.client ('authenticationFlights'). this.client () is a memoized constructor, it does not dial, so the flights get a Future map without a socket - needed because the binance futures/delivery user-data urls embed the listenKey, so no real ws client exists before the fetch - the flight is registered in client.subscriptions and the shared future is minted lazily by the first waiter via client.future (). an alone leader therefore has no future to reject, which removes the unhandled-rejection hazard the base version needed a silent .catch (() => {}) for - that arrow does not transpile (it crashes the php transpiler's regex chunker) and python's Future has no .catch at all - settlement deletes the map entry and then calls future.resolve / future.reject directly, matching the primitives' capture-delete-settle order. it deliberately does not use client.resolve / client.reject: those retain values in pendingResults / rejections for a later consumer, which is wrong for a one-shot auth flight - WsClient.close () now settles a client that never dialed. previously the socket teardown drove onClose -> reset -> reject, so a client with no connection left its futures pending and a waiter hung across close (). verified against master: the waiter stayed pending forever. python and php clients already cancel their futures on close, c# already rejects with ExchangeClosedByUser - javaTranspiler: the (String) cast for client.future (x) was hardcoded to the identifier `messageHash`; it now accepts any identifier so `flightHash` compiles. regenerating all 76 java ws exchanges produces a diff confined to the three files touched here, so the widening is a no-op for existing output verified: tsBuild 0 errors; eslint clean on all touched ts (the 2 WsClient warnings are pre-existing on master); test-base-ws-ts and test-base-ws-js both "base WS tests passed!"; negative control - sabotaging the guard in aster's acquire reds the wiring test with "got 3 fetches"; scoped transpile of binance/aster/bingx to all languages; php -l; py_compile on 3.12; go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction; go runtime probe of leader/waiter/resolve/re-acquire; gradlew :lib:compileJava BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Refs #29393 Refs #29903 * refactor(pro): inline the singleFlight helpers into authenticate Drop the four singleFlight* helper methods from binance/aster/bingx and paste their bodies straight into the authenticate () call sites. The behaviour is unchanged - same never-dialed this.client ('authenticationFlights'), same client.subscriptions registration flag, same lazily-minted shared future, same delete-then-settle ordering - but there is no longer a helper surface to keep in sync across three exchanges, and no base-class primitive to maintain for the six ports. The leader still never mints a future for itself, so an alone leader that rejects produces no unhandled rejection. test.singleFlightPrimitives.ts drove the now-deleted methods directly, so it is removed and its two unique cases are re-expressed through authenticate () in test.singleFlightWiring.ts: - solo-leader rejection (no waiter, no future minted, slot cleared, next caller re-leads, no unhandled rejection) - close () while a flight is in progress settles the waiter with ExchangeClosedByUser instead of stranding it Both new cases were verified to fail when their guard is removed: reverting the WsClient.close () never-dialed reset breaks the close case, and minting the future eagerly in the leader breaks the solo case. Refs #29393 * refactor(pro): route the inlined auth flight through client.futures the inlined single-flight block on binance/aster/bingx registered the flight with a boolean flag in client.subscriptions and settled it by reaching into client.futures to delete the entry and call future.resolve / future.reject on the captured object. that hand-rolled registry duplicates what Client already does and diverges from every other single-flight site in ts/src/pro. the flight now lives entirely in client.futures: - client.future () is the atomic check-and-insert, so the registration no longer needs a separate subscriptions flag that has to be kept in sync with the future map on all four exit paths - client.resolve () / client.reject () settle AND delete the entry themselves (Client.ts:160-189), so the manual `delete client.futures[hash]` blocks are gone - the leader mints its future BEFORE the request instead of leaving it to the first waiter. client.reject () parks the error in client.rejections[] when no future exists, and a parked rejection poisons the first waiter of the NEXT flight; because the leader always holds a future, reject always has a waiter and nothing is ever parked - the catch no longer rethrows: the trailing `await future` rethrows to the leader AND attaches the handler that keeps an alone leader's rejection from crashing node reusableFuture (), not future (): the two are identical in js/py/php/cs/java, but go's Client.Future () returns future.Await () - a `<-chan any` - while ReusableFuture () returns the *Future itself (exchange_client.go:130-138). the trailing await transpiles to `future.(*ccxt.Future).Await ()`, which panics on a channel. verified with a runtime probe against the go base: future() -> concrete type <-chan interface {} future() -> PANIC: interface conversion: interface {} is <-chan interface {}, not *ccxt.Future reusableFuture() -> concrete type *ccxt.Future reusableFuture() -> await OK, value=LISTEN-KEY-1 the wiring test asserts the new invariants: client.pendingResults and client.rejections must stay empty across a settled flight, a solo rejection and a fanned-out rejection, and close () must settle the leader's trailing await as well as the waiter. verified: tsc --noEmit 0 errors; tsBuild exit 0; test-base-ws-ts and test-base-ws-js both "base WS tests passed!" (js rebuilt first, the committed js/ was stale); negative control - replacing the `messageHash in client.futures` guard with `if (false)` reds the suite with "got 3 fetches" on bingx and again on aster, reverted after; scoped go transpile of binance/aster/bingx emits `ReusableFuture(messageHash)` + `future.(*ccxt.Future).Await()` and `go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction` exits 0; go runtime probe of the emitted shape shows leader await, waiter joining without a second fetch, and an empty futures map after settle. generated trees reverted, only ts/src is committed. eslint could not run - @typescript-eslint crashes with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'Cjs')" on an untouched file in a pristine checkout too, so it is pre-existing and unrelated. Refs #29393 Refs #29903 * fix(aster): unbreak PHP transpile of authenticate single-flight build/transpile.ts's PHP async rule `/\sawait\s+([^;]+);/g` is greedy and matches across newlines, so a COMMENT containing the bare token ` await ` starts a match inside the comment and swallows every following line up to the next `;`. On aster/binance/bingx the comment above the flight future did exactly that, wrapping `const future = client.reusableFuture (hash);` inside `Async\await( ... );` and emitting an unbalanced brace: PHP Parse error: Unclosed '{' on line 1378 does not match ')' Reword the six offending comments so the token `await` never appears in comment prose. No code shape changes: the authenticate () single-flight pattern (messageHash / reusableFuture / resolve / reject / trailing await) is untouched. Also sync with origin/master: #30008 removed Client.pendingResults, so test.singleFlightWiring.ts now counts parked work via client.rejections only, and the javaTranspiler Pattern 3 comment no longer cites the retired `flightHash` name. Verified: php -l clean on php/pro/{aster,binance,bingx}.php after a scoped transpile; npm run tsBuild passes; eslint 0 errors on every touched file; go build ./v4 ./v4/pro ./v4/prediction clean; 0 hits of singleFlightAcquire/Resolve/Reject across the regenerated php/cs/go/java/ js/python output for all three exchanges.
